decks.domain: Lane travel: curves, lane changes, passing, freeways and towing

cards.front: How far ahead should you scan for trouble spots, and why?
cards.back: Scan for trouble spots as far ahead as you can see, so you rarely need a last-minute move.

cards.front: What does good scanning take in, and what does it help you notice?
cards.back: Scanning means taking in the whole scene, roadsides included, so you notice pedestrians, hazards, vehicles that may cut into your path and signs routing you elsewhere.

cards.front: Which clues suggest a driver ahead may slow down or stop?
cards.back: Signs that a driver ahead may slow or stop include a cyclist or pedestrian on the road ahead, brake lights coming on and blinking turn signals.

cards.front: When should you slow for a curve, and what guides your speed?
cards.back: Slow down before entering a curve, using any speed posted under the curve sign as your guide.

cards.front: What should you do while driving through a curve?
cards.back: In a curve, look through it to your path, check where oncoming vehicles are in their lane, keep right of the center line in the middle of your lane, and expect hidden cyclists, pedestrians or slow vehicles.

cards.front: How should you change speed as you leave a curve?
cards.back: Speed up gradually as you leave a curve.

cards.front: What is the correct order of slowing and speeding up around a curve?
cards.back: Entering a curve you slow down first, while leaving a curve you build speed back up gradually, never the reverse.

cards.front: What is a blind spot, and how should you treat other drivers' blind spots?
cards.back: A blind spot is the area around a vehicle the driver cannot see from the seat even using mirrors, so avoid staying in another driver's blind spot.

cards.front: What steps come before changing lanes?
cards.back: Before changing lanes, signal, check your side and rearview mirrors for traffic coming from behind, and glance over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward.

cards.front: Why are mirrors alone not enough to clear a lane change, and which way do you glance?
cards.back: Mirrors alone do not clear a lane change, because the blind spot cannot be seen from the seat even with mirrors, so the shoulder glance goes toward the side you are moving to.

decks.domain: Lane travel: curves, lane changes, passing, freeways and towing

cards.front: What helps you pass safely, given that passing is routine but risky?
cards.back: Passing is routine but dangerous, so keep a good view ahead by not tailgating, especially trucks and trailers, and know how fast your vehicle can accelerate.

cards.front: What can go wrong if you return too early or too late after a pass, and what if you are unsure?
cards.back: Pass only with enough room: cutting back too early risks sideswiping the passed vehicle, returning too late risks a head-on crash, and when unsure you stay in your lane.

cards.front: What risk comes from cutting back in too soon after a pass, and from staying out too long?
cards.back: Cutting back in too soon after a pass risks sideswiping the vehicle you passed, while staying out too long risks a head-on crash with oncoming traffic.

cards.front: On a two-lane road, which side do you pass on, and where must the pass begin and end?
cards.back: On a two-lane road you pass only on the left, starting no sooner than the beginning of a passing zone and finishing before any no-passing zone.

cards.front: What fixes the start and the finish of a pass on a two-lane road?
cards.back: A pass must begin no earlier than the start of the passing zone and be finished before the no-passing zone, so both ends of the pass are fixed by the zone.

cards.front: May you go over the speed limit to finish a pass?
cards.back: You may not exceed the speed limit to pass, because going over the limit is illegal at all times.

cards.front: What are the steps of a pass, from checking the path to returning?
cards.back: To pass, confirm a clear path, check mirrors and glance over your shoulder toward the new lane, signal, speed up and finish quickly, then signal and return once the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror.

cards.front: After a pass, what tells you it is time to signal and move back?
cards.back: After a pass you signal and move back into your lane once the vehicle you passed is visible in your rearview mirror.

decks.domain: Lane travel: curves, lane changes, passing, freeways and towing

cards.front: How do you know where passing is allowed, and when must you never pass?
cards.back: Signs and pavement markings show where passing is allowed, and you must never pass where your view of oncoming traffic is limited.

cards.front: What two passing moves are banned around a no-passing zone?
cards.back: Do not cross the center line to pass inside a no-passing zone, and do not start a pass you cannot finish before reaching one.

cards.front: When does a hill or curve rule out passing?
cards.back: Do not pass when a hill or curve blocks your view of oncoming traffic.

cards.front: Near which road features is passing banned?
cards.back: Do not pass when approaching, at or inside an intersection or a railroad crossing.

cards.front: May you pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk?
cards.back: Do not pass a vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross.

cards.front: How does a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian at a crosswalk compare with other passing bans?
cards.back: Passing is banned when the vehicle ahead has stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian, just as it is banned near intersections and railroad crossings.

cards.front: In a no-passing zone, when may you cross the center line?
cards.back: In a no-passing zone you may cross the center line only when the right side of the road is blocked or when you are turning left.

cards.front: Which reasons allow crossing the center line in a no-passing zone, and which never does?
cards.back: In a no-passing zone, crossing the center line is still allowed to turn left or when the right side of the road is blocked, but never to pass.

decks.module: Passing on the right, being passed
decks.domain: Lane travel: curves, lane changes, passing, freeways and towing

cards.front: When may you pass a vehicle on the right that is turning left?
cards.back: You may pass on the right when the vehicle ahead is turning or signaling left, if there is room without leaving the pavement or using a bike lane and the road ahead of it is clear.

cards.front: On a road with two or more lanes your way, when may you pass on the right?
cards.back: You may also pass on the right on a road with two or more lanes in your direction when the vehicle you pass is in the left lane.

cards.front: How do the two cases for passing on the right differ?
cards.back: Passing a left-turning vehicle on the right is allowed only on pavement and outside the bike lane, whereas passing on the right on a multi-lane road needs the slower vehicle to be in the left lane.

cards.front: Why does passing on the right call for extra care, and how fast may you go?
cards.back: Take extra care when passing on the right, since other drivers do not expect it, and never speed past the limit to do it.

cards.front: What should you do while another vehicle passes you?
cards.back: When someone passes you, stay to the right, watch oncoming traffic and adjust your speed so the passer can get back into the right lane quickly.

cards.front: May you signal another driver when it is safe to pass?
cards.back: Never wave or use lights to tell other drivers when to pass; the law forbids flashing any of your signals for that purpose.

cards.front: How may you help a driver passing you, and what must you not do?
cards.back: When you are being passed, you help by keeping right and adjusting speed, but you must not wave the driver on or flash your signals to tell them when to go.

decks.domain: Lane travel: curves, lane changes, passing, freeways and towing

cards.front: Why does traffic usually flow better on freeways?
cards.back: Freeways have several lanes each way and higher speeds, and traffic flows better because access is controlled, sharp curves are few and there are no railroad crossings or traffic signals.

cards.front: Why hold a steady speed on a freeway instead of weaving?
cards.back: Holding a steady speed on a freeway reduces lane changes, while weaving through traffic raises crash risk and rarely saves time.

cards.front: How should your speed relate to freeway flow, and where do slower drivers go?
cards.back: Keep pace with traffic but do not exceed the posted speed to match the flow, and if you drive slower than the flow, use the right lane.

cards.front: Does keeping pace with freeway traffic ever allow exceeding the posted speed?
cards.back: Keeping pace with freeway traffic is encouraged, but the posted speed still caps you, and a driver below the flow belongs in the right lane.

cards.front: What should you do when vehicles are entering the freeway?
cards.back: Watch for vehicles entering the freeway and adjust your speed so they can merge smoothly.

cards.front: How do you warn drivers behind you that freeway traffic ahead is slowing?
cards.back: If you see freeway traffic slowing ahead, tap your brake pedal lightly several times to warn the drivers behind you.

cards.front: Which brake action warns the drivers behind you of freeway slowing?
cards.back: Several light taps on the brake pedal are how you warn drivers behind you that freeway traffic ahead is slowing.

cards.front: How does entering a freeway differ from entering most busy roads?
cards.back: Unlike entering most busy roads, you enter a freeway by using the on-ramp to speed up and merge with fast traffic.

cards.front: What do you do on the ramp instead of slowing or stopping?
cards.back: Entering a freeway is the reverse of entering most busy roads: instead of slowing or stopping, you speed up on the ramp and merge.

cards.front: What must you do when merging onto a freeway?
cards.back: When merging onto a freeway, yield to traffic already on it, check mirrors and blind spots, match its speed and keep moving, since drivers behind expect you to accelerate.

cards.front: What should you do if signs show you are entering a freeway the wrong way?
cards.back: If a DO NOT ENTER or WRONG WAY sign shows you are entering a freeway the wrong way, pull to the side of the ramp at once, stop, turn on hazard lights, and carefully turn around or back off the ramp.

decks.domain: Lane travel: curves, lane changes, passing, freeways and towing

cards.front: How do ramp meters work on single and multi-lane ramps?
cards.back: Ramp meters look like traffic signals and run only at certain times; on multi-lane ramps each lane has one, only one vehicle goes per green, and you speed up to merge when yours turns green.

cards.front: What should you do at a ramp meter that is dark?
cards.back: A dark ramp meter is not in use, so do not stop at it.

cards.front: How does a green ramp meter differ from a dark one?
cards.back: A ramp meter that shows green lets one vehicle go, while a dark ramp meter is off and requires no stop at all.
cards.memory_hook: green lets one, dark no stop

cards.front: How do you leave a freeway safely?
cards.back: To leave a freeway, signal well ahead, keep your speed until you are off the freeway, then slow to the posted advisory speed on the exit ramp.

cards.front: Where do you slow down when exiting a freeway?
cards.back: Leaving a freeway, you hold your speed until you are off the freeway and slow down only on the exit ramp, not in the travel lanes.

cards.front: What should you do if you miss your freeway exit?
cards.back: Most exits are numbered; if you miss yours, continue to the next one, because you must never stop or back up on a freeway and the shoulder is for emergencies only.

cards.front: What is allowed after missing an exit, and what is never allowed?
cards.back: A missed exit means driving on to the next one, while stopping or backing up on the freeway is never allowed and the shoulder is for emergencies only.

cards.front: What should you do if your vehicle has trouble on a freeway?
cards.back: With vehicle trouble on a freeway, move to the right shoulder or an emergency stopping area, turn on hazard lights, and if possible stay in or near the vehicle on the side away from traffic, since walking there is dangerous.

decks.domain: Lane travel: curves, lane changes, passing, freeways and towing

cards.front: How do large vehicles and vehicles towing trailers differ from cars?
cards.back: Large vehicles and vehicles towing trailers are longer, higher and wider, take longer to speed up and stop, and need more room to turn.

cards.front: What should you do when driving a camper, motor home or trailer and traffic builds behind?
cards.back: Driving a pickup with a camper, a motor home or a trailer, check your speed and the traffic behind often, pull off at the first safe turnout when traffic stacks up, and use the right lane on multi-lane roads.

cards.front: May passengers ride in a trailer, and are there exceptions?
cards.back: Letting passengers ride in a trailer is illegal, with three exceptions: a commercial bus trailer, a trailer that is independently steered, and a trailer towed by a fifth-wheel device.

cards.front: What must a fifth-wheel trailer have before it carries passengers?
cards.back: A fifth-wheel trailer carrying passengers needs safety glazing in its windows and windowed doors, a sound or visual signal to reach the driver, and a clear exit that opens from inside and outside.

cards.front: How does the passenger rule for a fifth-wheel trailer differ from ordinary trailers?
cards.back: A fifth-wheel trailer may carry passengers only when it has safety glazing, a way to signal the driver and an exit that opens from both sides, while trailers outside the listed exceptions may not carry passengers at all.

cards.front: How many boats, trailers or vehicles may a passenger or recreational vehicle tow in Oregon?
cards.back: Oregon law allows a passenger or recreational vehicle to tow at most one boat, utility trailer or other vehicle, so a second trailer or towed vehicle is not allowed.

cards.front: Is adding a second towed unit behind a passenger vehicle allowed?
cards.back: One boat, utility trailer or other vehicle may be towed behind a passenger or recreational vehicle, but adding a second towed unit is not allowed.

recap_hooks.text: Scan far ahead and across the whole scene, slow before a curve and build speed gradually as you leave it.
Before a lane change, signal, check both mirrors and glance over the shoulder toward the new lane, because mirrors cannot show the blind spot.
A pass needs a clear view, enough room and a legal speed, and it starts and ends inside the passing zone.
Return after a pass only when the passed vehicle appears in your rearview mirror, since cutting in early can sideswipe it.
Hills, curves, intersections, railroad crossings and crosswalk stops all rule out passing.
In a no-passing zone the center line may be crossed only to turn left or to get around a blocked right side.

recaps.module: Passing on the right, being passed

recap_hooks.text: Passing on the right is allowed around a left-turning vehicle with room on the pavement, or on a multi-lane road when the slower vehicle is in the left lane.
When someone passes you, keep right and adjust your speed, but never wave them on or flash your signals.
Hold a steady freeway speed within the posted limit, use the right lane if slower, and tap the brakes to warn of slowing ahead.
Enter a freeway by speeding up on the ramp, yielding to traffic already there and matching its speed.
A ramp meter lets one vehicle go on each green, and a dark meter means no stop.
Keep your speed until you are off the freeway, and after a missed exit drive on to the next one instead of stopping or backing up.
Large and towing vehicles need more time and room, so their drivers watch traffic behind and pull off at safe turnouts.
Trailer passengers are banned outside three exceptions, and a passenger or recreational vehicle may tow only one unit.
